title: The Handover That Did Not Share My Password
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Two weeks before my annual leave, my manager asked me to prepare a handover for the colleague covering my work.
Narrator: I first wrote a long document explaining every task, but the document was not enough. Several processes depended on accounts that only I could access.
Narrator: [carefully] A teammate suggested sending him my password for the month. It sounded quick, yet it would remove accountability and might violate our security policy.
Narrator: Instead, I listed the work functions he needed and asked the system owners to create approved access under his own identity.
Narrator: [reflective] They gave him only the permissions required for the temporary role and recorded an end date for the access.
Narrator: We tested the main tasks together using sample or permitted data, not real customer information copied into a training file.
Narrator: [honestly] The handover document explained deadlines, decision rules, contact points, current risks, and which situations required approval.
Narrator: It did not include secret keys, passwords, unnecessary personal details, or confidential notes about colleagues.
Narrator: [seriously] For one older system, separate access could not be arranged before my leave. We did not work around the control.
Narrator: My manager reassigned that task to an authorized employee and told clients how urgent requests would be handled.
Narrator: [gently] We also agreed that I would not monitor routine messages during leave. A genuine emergency had a documented escalation route that did not depend on my private telephone.
Narrator: On my last working day, my colleague completed a test task while I observed. His questions revealed two instructions that had made sense only in my head.
Narrator: [encouraging] I rewrote them with examples and added the location of the official policy rather than relying on memory.
Narrator: When I returned, no one had used my account, and the temporary access had ended as scheduled.
Narrator: [sincere] There had been one delay, but the record showed who made each decision and why.
Narrator: A good handover does more than keep work moving. It protects security, preserves accountability, respects leave, and makes hidden knowledge understandable to someone else.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator refuse to share a password?
options: The colleague had forgotten his name
It would weaken accountability and could violate policy
The password was too long to type
Annual leave prevents all system use
quiz.explanation: Each person needed approved access under their own identity.

quiz.question: How was temporary access limited?
options: By required permissions and an end date
By using customer data for practice
quiz.explanation: Least privilege and expiry reduced risk.

quiz.question: What did the handover exclude?
quiz.explanation: Useful instructions were separated from secrets.

quiz.question: How was the unsupported older-system task handled?
options: It was reassigned to someone already authorized
quiz.explanation: The team did not solve urgency by breaking access rules.

quiz.question: What improved during the test task?
options: Two unclear instructions were rewritten with examples

quiz.question: Why did the long document fail by itself?
options: The covering colleague lacked approved access to required systems
quiz.explanation: Knowledge and authorization were separate needs.

quiz.question: Why did the team use sample or permitted data?
options: Training did not justify copying real customer information

quiz.question: What protected the narrator’s leave?
options: A promise to check every message
A documented emergency route that did not depend on routine personal contact
quiz.explanation: Continuity was designed without erasing time off.

quiz.question: What does the one delay show?
options: Password sharing would prevent every delay
A controlled process may still have imperfection while preserving accountability
quiz.explanation: Reliability is not the same as zero friction.

quiz.question: Which four aims close the account?
options: Security, accountability, respected leave, and understandable knowledge
quiz.explanation: The conclusion names the handover’s wider value.
